claim: Diabetes affects more than 34 million adults in the United States in 2020.
source: Diabetes, a disease characterized by high blood glucose levels, is one of the most common chronic diseases in the United States, affecting more than 34 million adults in 2020 (CDC, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to CDC, 2020.

claim: In healthy people, blood glucose levels are regulated by the hormone insulin through a negative feedback loop.
source: In healthy people, blood glucose levels are regulated by the hormone insulin through a negative feedback loop.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about insulin's role in glucose homeostasis.

claim: High blood glucose promotes the secretion of insulin from the β-cells of the pancreas.
source: High blood glucose promotes the secretion of insulin from the β-cells of the pancreas.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the glucose-insulin feedback loop.

claim: Insulin lowers blood glucose by suppressing glucose production and promoting glucose uptake.
source: Insulin, in turn, lowers blood glucose by suppressing glucose production (e.g., in the liver) and promoting glucose uptake (e.g., by the muscle).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about insulin's physiological effects.

claim: Diabetes is associated with defects in the homeostatic feedback loop involving insulin and glucose.
source: Thus, diabetes is associated with defects in this homeostatic feedback loop (DeFronzo, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to DeFronzo, 1988.

claim: In type 1 diabetes, autoimmune destruction of β-cells results in a complete lack of insulin production and dependence on insulin treatment for survival.
source: In T1D, autoimmune destruction of the β-cells results in a complete lack of insulin production, and thus dependence on insulin treatment for survival (Katsarou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Katsarou et al., 2017.

claim: In type 2 diabetes, autoimmunity is not present.
source: In T2D, such autoimmunity is not present.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge distinguishing T2D from T1D.

claim: Type 2 diabetes is generally viewed as a progressive disease in which blood glucose control gradually worsens over the course of years.
source: T2D is generally viewed as a progressive disease, in which blood glucose control gradually worsens over the course of years.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T2D progression.

claim: In the early stages of type 2 diabetes pathogenesis, the body produces insulin but its ability to reduce blood glucose levels is inadequate (insulin resistance).
source: In the early stages of T2D pathogenesis, the body produces insulin, but its ability to reduce blood glucose levels is inadequate (insulin resistance).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about early T2D.

claim: In later stages of type 2 diabetes, insulin production declines, eventually leading to dependence on insulin treatment.
source: In later stages of T2D, insulin production declines, eventually leading to dependence on insulin treatment (DeFronzo et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to DeFronzo et al., 2015.

claim: Short-timescale models describe the dynamics of insulin and glucose over minutes or hours.
source: Short-timescale models describe the dynamics of insulin and glucose over minutes or hours (Bergman et al., 1979; Cobelli et al., 2014; Toffolo et al., 1995; Toffolo et al., 2001; Stefanovski et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to modeling literature.

claim: Short-timescale models describe a negative feedback loop where glucose promotes insulin secretion and insulin promotes glucose disposal.
source: These models describe a negative feedback loop, where glucose promotes insulin secretion and insulin promotes glucose disposal.
evidence: This is a description of established mathematical models in the field.

claim: Short-timescale models have been used extensively in the interpretation of physiological measurements, for example, to infer insulin sensitivity on the basis of glucose tolerance tests.
source: Such models have been used extensively in the interpretation of physiological measurements, for example, to infer insulin sensitivity on the basis of glucose tolerance tests (Bergman et al., 1979; Dalla Man et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bergman et al., 1979 and Dalla Man et al., 2002.

claim: A second class of models integrates simple short-timescale models with processes that occur on longer timescales of months to years, with the goal of describing type 2 diabetes pathogenesis.
source: A second class of models integrates simple short-timescale models with processes that occur on longer timescales of months to years, with the goal of describing T2D pathogenesis (Topp et al., 2000; Ha et al., 2016; Ha and Sherman, 2020; Karin et al., 2016; De Gaetano and Hardy, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to modeling literature.

claim: Long-timescale models generally include an adaptive process where either slightly elevated glucose or per-β-cell insulin secretion prompts increases in β-cell activity or mass.
source: These models generally include an adaptive process, where either slightly elevated glucose or per-β-cell insulin secretion prompts increases in β-cell activity or mass, and a glucotoxicity process, where severely elevated glucose causes death or deactivation of β-cells.
evidence: This is a description of established mathematical models in the field.

claim: Long-timescale models generally include a glucotoxicity process where severely elevated glucose causes death or deactivation of β-cells.
source: These models generally include an adaptive process, where either slightly elevated glucose or per-β-cell insulin secretion prompts increases in β-cell activity or mass, and a glucotoxicity process, where severely elevated glucose causes death or deactivation of β-cells.
evidence: This is a description of established mathematical models in the field.

claim: Evidence suggests that β-cells do not proliferate appreciably in adults.
source: Adaptation may involve increases in mass or secretory function of individual cells or it may include cell division that can eventually produce recovery from death of cells (Topp et al., 2000; Ha et al., 2016), but evidence suggests that -cells do not proliferate appreciably in adults (Cnop et al., 2010; Saisho et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cnop et al., 2010 and Saisho et al., 2013.

claim: Type 2 diabetes of short duration can generally be reversed by interventions which improve insulin resistance and secretion.
source: Whether or not some amount of proliferation can occur, it is empirically true that T2D of short duration can generally be reversed by interventions which improve insulin resistance and secretion, while T2D of longer duration which has advanced to severe hyperglycemia cannot be reversed (UK Prospective Diabetes Study Group, 1995; Turner, 1999), a fact which is explained by existing models since they connect severe hyperglycemia to severe losses of β-cells (Ha et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to UK Prospective Diabetes Study Group, 1995 and Turner, 1999.

claim: Type 2 diabetes of longer duration which has advanced to severe hyperglycemia cannot be reversed.
source: Whether or not some amount of proliferation can occur, it is empirically true that T2D of short duration can generally be reversed by interventions which improve insulin resistance and secretion, while T2D of longer duration which has advanced to severe hyperglycemia cannot be reversed (UK Prospective Diabetes Study Group, 1995; Turner, 1999), a fact which is explained by existing models since they connect severe hyperglycemia to severe losses of β-cells (Ha et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to UK Prospective Diabetes Study Group, 1995 and Turner, 1999.

claim: Existing models explain the irreversibility of advanced type 2 diabetes by connecting severe hyperglycemia to severe losses of β-cells.
source: Whether or not some amount of proliferation can occur, it is empirically true that T2D of short duration can generally be reversed by interventions which improve insulin resistance and secretion, while T2D of longer duration which has advanced to severe hyperglycemia cannot be reversed (UK Prospective Diabetes Study Group, 1995; Turner, 1999), a fact which is explained by existing models since they connect severe hyperglycemia to severe losses of β-cells (Ha et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ha et al., 2016.

claim: Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes is a subtype of type 2 diabetes common in particular in patients of African descent.
source: The focus of this work is on ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes (KPD), a subtype of T2D, common in particular in patients of African descent (Vellanki and Umpierrez, 2017; Umpierrez et al., 1995; McFarlane et al., 2001; Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes presents with ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis, an episode of extremely high blood glucose and low blood pH due to excess ketone bodies.
source: KPD presents with ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), an episode of extremely high blood glucose and low blood pH due to excess ketone bodies.
evidence: This is a description of the clinical presentation of KPD.

claim: In ketosis-prone diabetes, β-cell autoimmunity is not present.
source: Unlike in T1D, however, β-cell autoimmunity is not present in KPD.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about KPD.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes patients can often achieve partial remission after a few weeks or months of treatment with insulin.
source: Further, KPD patients can often achieve partial remission: after a few weeks or months of treatment with insulin, they are no longer dependent on insulin and can control blood glucose with diet or oral antidiabetic agents (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b; McFarlane et al., 2001; Vellanki et al., 2016; Umpierrez et al., 1997; Vellanki et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is substantial heterogeneity in response to insulin treatment among ketosis-prone diabetes patients.
source: There is substantial heterogeneity in response to insulin treatment.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about KPD patients.

claim: Some ketosis-prone diabetes patients are unable to achieve remission.
source: Firstly, some patients are unable to achieve remission.
evidence: This is stated as a clinical observation about KPD patients.

claim: When remission is achieved in ketosis-prone diabetes, it does not always last, with duration varying from 6 months to 10 years.
source: Secondly, when remission is achieved, it does not always last: the duration of the remission (the time until a patient's condition worsens to the point where they again require insulin) varies from 6 months to 10 years (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes patients generally report less than 4 weeks of diabetes-associated symptoms prior to the emergency.
source: Although no study has systematically characterized the duration of high blood glucose preceding the acute DKA event, patients generally report less than 4 weeks of diabetes-associated symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss) prior to the emergency (Vellanki and Umpierrez, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vellanki and Umpierrez, 2017.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes is associated with obesity and insulin resistance.
source: Associated with obesity and insulin resistance (Umpierrez et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Umpierrez et al., 1995 in Table 1.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes has potentially rapid onset of hyperglycemic crisis.
source: Potentially rapid onset of hyperglycemic crisis (Umpierrez et al., 1995; Vellanki and Umpierrez, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Umpierrez et al., 1995 and Vellanki and Umpierrez, 2017 in Table 1.

claim: Onset of hyperglycemic crisis in ketosis-prone diabetes is associated with a period of high sugar consumption.
source: Onset of hyperglycemic crisis associated with period of high sugar consumption (this is a common observation in our (PV) clinic, but it is difficult to test its statistical significance because antecedent data for new-onset diabetes are usually unavailable)
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observations from the authors' clinic.

claim: Ketotic relapses in ketosis-prone diabetes are preceded by a period of hyperglycemia.
source: Ketotic relapses are preceded by a period of hyperglycemia (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b in Table 1.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes patients have poor β-cell function at presentation.
source: Poor β-cell function at presentation (Umpierrez et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Umpierrez et al., 1995 in Table 1.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes patients show improvement of β-cell function with weeks or months of insulin treatment.
source: Improvement of β-cell function with weeks or months of insulin treatment (Umpierrez et al., 1995; McFarlane et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Umpierrez et al., 1995 and McFarlane et al., 2001 in Table 1.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes patients show worsening of β-cell function after many hours of glucose infusion.
source: Worsening of β-cell function after many hours of glucose infusion (Umpierrez et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Umpierrez et al., 2007 in Table 1.

claim: There is patient-to-patient variation in ability to achieve and sustain remission in ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: Patient-to-patient variation in ability to achieve and sustain remission (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b; McFarlane et al., 2001; Vellanki et al., 2016; Umpierrez et al., 1997; Vellanki et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations in Table 1.

claim: Duration of remission in ketosis-prone diabetes is improved by non-insulin blood glucose management due to greater β-cell function.
source: Duration of remission is improved by (non-insulin) blood glucose management due to greater β-cell function (Vellanki et al., 2016; Umpierrez et al., 1997; Vellanki et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations in Table 1.

claim: Long-term declines in insulin sensitivity and secretion in ketosis-prone diabetes are similar to conventional type 2 diabetes.
source: Long-term declines in insulin sensitivity and secretion are similar to 'conventional' type 2 diabetes (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b; Banerji et al., 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004b and Banerji et al., 1996 in Table 1.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes patients with less insulin resistance have lower glucose in remission.
source: Patients with less insulin resistance have lower glucose in remission, although it is unclear if this predicts long-term prognosis (Vellanki et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vellanki et al., 2020 in Table 1.

claim: Existing models of diabetes pathogenesis, in which β-cell deactivation occurs slowly over months and is often thought to be irreversible, cannot account for the phenomena of ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: Existing models of diabetes pathogenesis, in which β-cell deactivation occurs slowly over months and is often thought to be irreversible, cannot account for these phenomena.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of existing models with KPD phenomenology.

claim: The possibility of rapid onset of severe hyperglycemia and rapid remission of ketosis-prone diabetes suggests the existence of a faster pathogenic mechanism operating on timescales of days or weeks.
source: Instead, the possibility of rapid onset of severe hyperglycemia and rapid remission of KPD suggests the existence of a faster pathogenic mechanism, operating on timescales of days or weeks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical observations of KPD.

claim: In an experiment where a ketosis-prone diabetes patient was given a 20-hour infusion of glucose, their level of insulin secretion dropped by about a factor of two over the course of the infusion.
source: Indeed, in an experiment where a KPD patient was given a 20-hour infusion of glucose, it was observed that their level of insulin secretion (but not that of a control) dropped by about a factor of two over the course of the infusion (Umpierrez et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Umpierrez et al., 2007.

claim: The authors propose that ketosis-prone diabetes differs from conventional type 2 diabetes through the presence of a second type of glucotoxicity, which is fast but reversible.
source: We thus propose that KPD differs from conventional T2D through the presence of a second type of glucotoxicity, which is fast but reversible.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The fast, reversible glucotoxicity mechanism may also be present, but merely less pronounced, in type 2 diabetes patients who do not show features of ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: This mechanism may also be present, but merely less pronounced, in T2D patients who do not show features of KPD.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the authors' hypothesis.

claim: The mathematical model described by Equations 1-5 incorporates the assumption of a fast, reversible glucotoxicity process.
source: Adding this mechanism to the existing view of diabetes pathogenesis, we arrive at a mathematical model depicted in Figure 1 and described by Equations 1–5 ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of the model developed in the manuscript.

claim: The model simulations only simulate patients in advanced prediabetes, where β-cells have already maximized their secretory capacity.
source: Below we only simulate patients in advanced prediabetes, where we presume that β-cells have already maximized their secretory capacity, so that the adaptive process in Figure 1C is saturated.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the simulations.

claim: The glycemic emergency or diabetic ketoacidosis in ketosis-prone diabetes is often preceded by a period of high sugar consumption.
source: Since the glycemic emergency or DKA in KPD is often preceded by a period of high sugar consumption (Table 1, criterion 3), and in past experiments such patients show reductions in β-cell function during a period of glucose infusion (Umpierrez et al., 2007), we simulate a period of a month of increased sugar consumption.
evidence: This is based on clinical observations and cited experimental data.

claim: Insulin treatment carried out until blood glucose is well controlled produces a remission of dramatic hyperglycemia in the model.
source: Insulin treatment, carried out until blood glucose is well controlled (between the blue lines), produces a remission of this dramatic hyperglycemia, returning the glucose to its value before the period of high sugar consumption.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The model reproduces the qualitative features associated with ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: We thus see that our model reproduces the qualitative features associated with KPD.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: The model can produce heterogeneous patient outcomes with different parameter values.
source: Further, the model can produce heterogeneous patient outcomes: the time required to achieve remission and the possibility of relapse are different for different parameter values (Table 1, criterion 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results showing different outcomes.

claim: In the model, failure to maintain remission emerges from glucotoxicity, consistent with the observation that better blood-glucose management increases the duration of remission.
source: Since a failure to maintain remission emerges from glucotoxicity in this model, it is also consistent with the observation that better blood-glucose management increases the duration of remission (Table 1, criterion 9).
evidence: This is an inference connecting model behavior to clinical observations.

claim: The onset and remission seen in the model simulations are reminiscent of bistability in dynamical systems.
source: The onset and remission seen in our simulations are reminiscent of bistability in dynamical systems: the blood glucose in the KPD patients in this model seems to have two stable values, with transitions between the two triggered by intense glucose consumption or insulin treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model behavior.

claim: Bistability is often associated with positive feedback loops.
source: Indeed, since bistability is often associated with positive feedback loops (Alon, 2019), and the reversible inactivation of β-cells by glucose creates such a loop, it is natural to expect such a behavior.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynamical systems, supported by a citation to Alon, 2019.

claim: The reversible inactivation of β-cells by glucose creates a positive feedback loop.
source: Indeed, since bistability is often associated with positive feedback loops (Alon, 2019), and the reversible inactivation of β-cells by glucose creates such a loop, it is natural to expect such a behavior.
evidence: This is an inference about the model structure.

claim: The behavior of the model for ketosis-prone diabetes parameter values is a classic 'toggle switch'.
source: This behavior is a classic 'toggle switch' (Gardner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a characterization of the model behavior, supported by a citation to Gardner et al., 2000.

claim: There is a threshold value of the ratio of inactivation to reactivation rates above which there is no healthy state and thus a complete loss of β-cell function.
source: Similarly, there is a second threshold above which there is no healthy state, and thus a complete loss of β-cell function.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Improvements in insulin sensitivity can produce a partial remission in the model.
source: Thus, improvements in insulin sensitivity can produce a partial remission, and death of β-cells can prevent remission.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Death of β-cells can prevent remission in the model.
source: Thus, improvements in insulin sensitivity can produce a partial remission, and death of β-cells can prevent remission.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The boundaries of the bistable regions in the model roughly follow the contours of fasting glucose.
source: We see in Figure 6 that the boundaries of the hatched regions roughly follow the contours of fasting glucose.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: If the parameters of the model could be accurately measured in a patient, the model would predict the course of remission for a given insulin treatment schedule.
source: Finally, we note that, if the parameters of this model could be accurately measured in a patient, then the model would predict the course of remission for a given insulin treatment schedule, and thus assist in designing treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications of the model.

claim: In the model, tighter insulin control will always produce a faster remission.
source: In this model, tighter insulin control will always produce a faster remission.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: The optimal treatment protocol in the model is to pick a safe target fasting glucose which avoids the risk of hypoglycemia, and then titrate the insulin dose to achieve this target glucose.
source: Thus, the optimal treatment protocol (assuming glucose consumption is minimized) is to pick a safe target fasting glucose which avoids the risk of hypoglycemia, and then titrate the insulin dose to achieve this target glucose.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: Remission is only achieved in the model if a fasting glucose value lower than the stable fixed-point value is targeted during insulin treatment.
source: Remission is only achieved if a value lower than the stable fixed-point value (which, for this patient, is 110 mg/dL) is targeted, and lower glucose targets produce a faster remission.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Lower glucose targets produce a faster remission in the model.
source: Remission is only achieved if a value lower than the stable fixed-point value (which, for this patient, is 110 mg/dL) is targeted, and lower glucose targets produce a faster remission.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The model predicts that achieving a given target fasting glucose requires an insulin dose that starts high and is decreased exponentially over time.
source: We see that, because of the improvement in β-cell function over the course of treatment, the model predicts that achieving a given target requires an insulin dose that starts high and is decreased exponentially over time.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Other parameters such as total β-cell population and insulin resistance are predicted to be associated with both ketosis-prone diabetes and conventional type 2 diabetes.
source: Other parameters, such as the total β-cell population and insulin resistance, are predicted to be associated with both KPD and 'conventional' T2D.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model analysis.

claim: A lower total β-cell reserve is associated with both the appearance of ketosis-prone diabetes and difficulty in achieving remission.
source: In particular, since a lower total β-cell reserve is associated with both the appearance of KPD and difficulty in achieving remission, a period of uncontrolled T2D, even conventional T2D, during which the slow glucotoxicity will reduce the number of β-cells, can lead to the onset of KPD and is predicted to make recovery less likely.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model analysis.

claim: A period of uncontrolled type 2 diabetes can lead to the onset of ketosis-prone diabetes and is predicted to make recovery less likely.
source: In particular, since a lower total β-cell reserve is associated with both the appearance of KPD and difficulty in achieving remission, a period of uncontrolled T2D, even conventional T2D, during which the slow glucotoxicity will reduce the number of β-cells, can lead to the onset of KPD and is predicted to make recovery less likely.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model analysis.

claim: Practical usage of the model in the clinic will require assessing which parameters vary substantially in the population and developing protocols to measure those which vary in individual patients.
source: Practical usage of this model in the clinic will require both assessing which of these parameters vary substantially in the population and developing protocols to measure those which vary in individual patients.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed for clinical application.

claim: Very little is known about specific genetic factors which predispose individuals to ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: Although KPD is more prevalent in specific ethnic groups, very little is known about specific genetic factors which predispose individuals to KPD.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: A pax4 allele specific to West African populations seems to be associated with ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: A pax4 allele specific to West African populations seems to be associated with KPD, with a small number of monozygous individuals found in a sample of KPD patients and none in control individuals or those with conventional T2D (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004a.

claim: PAX4 is expressed during the development of pancreatic islets.
source: Since PAX4 is expressed during the development of pancreatic islets, where β-cells are located, it was hypothesized that this variant acts either through an effect on the total number of β-cells formed or through the formation of defective -cells (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2004a.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes is associated with deficiency in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.
source: Other work has found that KPD is associated with deficiency in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme which plays a role in reducing oxidative stress, which is consistent with a mechanism where this reversible glucotoxicity is mediated by oxidative stress (Sobngwi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sobngwi et al., 2005.

claim: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase plays a role in reducing oxidative stress.
source: Other work has found that KPD is associated with deficiency in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme which plays a role in reducing oxidative stress, which is consistent with a mechanism where this reversible glucotoxicity is mediated by oxidative stress (Sobngwi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: The association of ketosis-prone diabetes with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is consistent with a mechanism where reversible glucotoxicity is mediated by oxidative stress.
source: Other work has found that KPD is associated with deficiency in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme which plays a role in reducing oxidative stress, which is consistent with a mechanism where this reversible glucotoxicity is mediated by oxidative stress (Sobngwi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the genetic association to a potential mechanism.

claim: Ketosis-prone diabetes patients tend to have a family history of diabetes.
source: The fact that KPD patients tend to have a family history of diabetes (Umpierrez et al., 1995) is also consistent with genetic variation in the rate of reversible inactivation of β-cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Umpierrez et al., 1995.

claim: The fact that ketosis-prone diabetes patients tend to have a family history of diabetes is consistent with genetic variation in the rate of reversible inactivation of β-cells.
source: The fact that KPD patients tend to have a family history of diabetes (Umpierrez et al., 1995) is also consistent with genetic variation in the rate of reversible inactivation of β-cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the family history observation to the model's predictions.

claim: If the reversible activation process is present in all individuals with a heterogeneous rate, then conventional type 2 diabetes may always involve some degree of reversible inactivation, with ketosis-prone diabetes representing only the extreme end of a continuum.
source: If, as we hypothesize, the reversible activation process is present in all individuals, with a heterogeneous rate, then it is possible that 'conventional' T2D always involves some degree of reversible inactivation, with KPD representing only the extreme end of a continuum.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the model.

claim: The hypothesis that reversible inactivation exists on a continuum may explain observations of partial remission after insulin treatment in populations with more conventional forms of type 2 diabetes.
source: This may explain observations of partial remission after insulin treatment in populations with more conventional forms of T2D (Ryan et al., 2004; Weng et al., 2008; Retnakaran et al., 2010; Retnakaran et al., 2014; Kramer et al., 2013a; Kramer et al., 2013b; Chon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of clinical observations, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Others have argued that data on partial remission in type 2 diabetes are evidence of the reversal of glucotoxicity.
source: In fact, others have also argued that these data are evidence of the reversal of glucotoxicity (Retnakaran et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Retnakaran et al., 2024.

claim: The 'honeymoon phase' in type 1 diabetes may involve some component of glucotoxicity reversal.
source: Although T1D is primarily driven by immune destruction of β-cells, the 'honeymoon phase', where symptoms temporarily improve upon insulin treatment, may involve some component of glucotoxicity reversal.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about T1D.

claim: Instances of diabetes remission produced by dramatic changes in insulin resistance may involve some component of glucotoxicity reversal.
source: Further, instances of diabetes remission produced by dramatic changes in insulin resistance (such as recovery from gestational diabetes postpartum, or reversal of T2D through very low-calorie diets) may also involve some component of glucotoxicity reversal.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about other forms of diabetes remission.

claim: The rapid progression of type 2 diabetes in youth may possibly be understood using models like the one discussed through person-to-person variation in the rate of permanent β-cell deactivation.
source: Other phenomena, like the rapid (and difficult-to-reverse) progression of T2D in youth (Utzschneider et al., 2021), may possibly be understood using models like the one discussed here through person-to-person variation in the rate of permanent β-cell deactivation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about T2D in youth, with a citation to Utzschneider et al., 2021.

claim: The model is consistent with the observation that a similar remission is seen in insulin treatment of patients with similar demographics to ketosis-prone diabetes patients who present with severe hyperglycemia but not ketoacidosis.
source: A period of extreme hyperglycemia and low insulin secretion does not guarantee the presence of ketoacidosis. Thus, our model is consistent with the observation that a similar remission is seen in insulin treatment of patients with similar demographics to KPD patients who present with severe hyperglycemia, but not ketoacidosis (Umpierrez et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's consistency with clinical observations, supported by a citation to Umpierrez et al., 1995.

claim: It has been proposed that insulin resistance may adaptively change in response to levels of insulin or glucose.
source: It has been proposed in the past that insulin resistance may adaptively change in response to levels of insulin or glucose (Rossetti et al., 1987; DeFronzo, 1988; Ader et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rossetti et al., 1987, DeFronzo, 1988, and Ader et al., 2014.

claim: Insulin treatment is associated with reductions in insulin resistance.
source: Although insulin treatment is associated with reductions in insulin resistance (Umpierrez et al., 1995; Scarlett et al., 1982), this effect is likely downstream of glucose levels: insulin itself has been proposed to promote insulin resistance (Ader et al., 2014; DeFronzo, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Umpierrez et al., 1995 and Scarlett et al., 1982.

claim: The effect of insulin treatment on insulin resistance is likely downstream of glucose levels.
source: Although insulin treatment is associated with reductions in insulin resistance (Umpierrez et al., 1995; Scarlett et al., 1982), this effect is likely downstream of glucose levels: insulin itself has been proposed to promote insulin resistance (Ader et al., 2014; DeFronzo, 1988).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: Insulin itself has been proposed to promote insulin resistance.
source: Although insulin treatment is associated with reductions in insulin resistance (Umpierrez et al., 1995; Scarlett et al., 1982), this effect is likely downstream of glucose levels: insulin itself has been proposed to promote insulin resistance (Ader et al., 2014; DeFronzo, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ader et al., 2014 and DeFronzo, 1988.

claim: If remission is produced by insulin per se rather than normoglycemia, it would likely be mediated by insulin acting directly on β-cells to promote insulin secretion.
source: Thus, if remission is produced by insulin per se rather than normoglycemia, it would likely be mediated by insulin acting directly on β-cells to promote insulin secretion, as suggested, for example, by experiments where β-cell specific insulin receptor knockouts show a reduction in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Kulkarni et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative inference, supported by a citation to Kulkarni et al., 1999.

claim: β-cell specific insulin receptor knockouts show a reduction in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: Thus, if remission is produced by insulin per se rather than normoglycemia, it would likely be mediated by insulin acting directly on β-cells to promote insulin secretion, as suggested, for example, by experiments where β-cell specific insulin receptor knockouts show a reduction in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Kulkarni et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kulkarni et al., 1999.

claim: Due to the much lower relative concentration of insulin produced in the islets by exogenous insulin administration rather than endogenous insulin, it seems unlikely that remission is produced by insulin acting directly on β-cells.
source: On the other hand, due to the much lower relative concentration of insulin produced in the islets by exogenous insulin administration rather than endogenous insulin (Unger and Cherrington, 2012), this seems unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference based on physiological considerations, supported by a citation to Unger and Cherrington, 2012.

claim: The qualitative success of the model suggests that multiple distinct types of glucotoxicity may operate in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes and ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: The qualitative success of our model suggests that multiple distinct types of glucotoxicity may operate in the pathogenesis of T2D and KPD: a slower, irreversible death of β-cells which is responsible for slow, irreversible decline in T2D and failure to maintain or achieve remission in KPD, and a faster, reversible process associated with rapid onset and remission of KPD.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model's ability to reproduce KPD phenomenology.

claim: The clearest test of the model would be a cellular or systems-biology-based identification and characterization of multiple β-cell states and inactivation mechanisms, all dependent on glucose level.
source: The clearest test of our model would be a cellular or systems-biology-based identification and characterization of multiple β-cell states and inactivation mechanisms, all dependent on glucose level.
evidence: This is a statement about how the model could be tested.

claim: Some studies have shown diversity of β-cell secretory phenotypes and transition between phenotypes in a glucose-dependent way.
source: Some pioneering studies along these lines have been done already, showing diversity of β-cell secretory phenotypes and transition between phenotypes in a glucose-dependent way (Miranda et al., 2021; Laybutt et al., 2002; Jonas et al., 1999; Laybutt et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2014; Dahan et al., 2017), though mostly in rodent models.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Experiments show that roughly 2-4 weeks of hyperglycemia can change gene expression and secretory phenotypes in β-cells, and then normoglycemia can restore normal function on similar scales.
source: Such experiments show that roughly 2–4 weeks of hyperglycemia can change gene expression and secretory phenotypes in β-cells, and then normoglycemia can restore normal function on similar scales (Laybutt et al., 2002; Jonas et al., 1999; Laybutt et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Laybutt et al., 2002, Jonas et al., 1999, and Laybutt et al., 2003.

claim: There is evidence that reversible glucotoxicity of a type similar to what is described in the model exists in rodents.
source: Thus, there is evidence that reversible glucotoxicity, of a type similar to what we have described, exists in rodents.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cited experimental evidence.

claim: The model predicts that the rates of β-cell activation and deactivation should correlate with the predisposition to ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: Crucially, it remains to be seen if the rates of β-cell activation and deactivation in such experiments in humans would correlate with the predisposition to KPD, which is a clear prediction of our model.
evidence: This is a stated prediction of the model.

claim: Producing bistability in the model requires that total insulin secretion decreases as glucose is increased for some values of glucose.
source: Producing bistability requires that, after allowing glucotoxicity processes to equilibrate, total insulin secretion decreases as glucose is increased, for some values of glucose.
evidence: This is a mathematical requirement derived from the model structure.

claim: The rate of reversible inactivation in the model is roughly consistent with the limited existing data in ketosis-prone diabetes patients.
source: Thus, our rate of reversible inactivation is roughly consistent with the limited existing data in KPD patients.
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: The model generally produces bistability only when glucose is already at least slightly elevated.
source: As seen in Figure 6, our model generally produces bistability only when glucose is already at least slightly elevated.
evidence: This is an observation from the model analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Within the model, the onset of ketosis-prone diabetes crucially depends on the β-cell adaptation mechanisms having reached nearly maximum adaptation, and then the patient undergoing a period of high carbohydrate consumption.
source: In other words, within our model, the onset of KPD crucially depends on the β-cell adaptation mechanisms having reached nearly maximum adaptation, and then the patient undergoing a period of high carbohydrate consumption.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the model's requirements for KPD onset.

claim: The model suggests that limiting carbohydrates per se would be advisable for ketosis-prone diabetes patients.
source: Our model, however, would suggest that limiting carbohydrates per se, as in T1D, would also be advisable.
evidence: This is an inference from the model about clinical recommendations.

claim: Patient-specific fits of a more detailed version of the model could provide personalized clinical guidance on insulin treatment.
source: In the longer term, patient-specific fits of a more detailed version of this model could provide personalized clinical guidance on insulin treatment, as suggested by Figure 7.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future clinical applications.

claim: Simple models can be useful both for basic biomedical science and in the clinic.
source: While simple models of the type that we developed here are certainly wrong in that they do not account for the full complexity of the underlying physiology, they can be useful both for basic biomedical science and in the clinic.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of mathematical models.

claim: The model predicts new β-cell states and activation/deactivation processes.
source: Specifically, they predict new β-cell states and activation/deactivation processes, and hence tell us to look for diversity of β-cell phenotypes.
evidence: This is a statement about what the model predicts.

claim: The model suggests that clinical practice should be modified to include more frequent follow-ups or continuous monitoring to generate data on temporal scales that match the dynamics of the model.
source: They also suggest that clinical practice should be modified to include more frequent follow-ups (or continuous monitoring) to generate data on temporal scales that match the dynamics of the model.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model's temporal dynamics.

claim: The model proposes key mechanisms (rates of secretory phenotype switching) that might determine predisposition to ketosis-prone diabetes.
source: And they propose key mechanisms (rates of secretory phenotype switching) that might determine predisposition to KPD, which also can be accessed experimentally or even clinically.
evidence: This is a statement about what the model proposes.

claim: The simplicity of the model makes it plausible that the proposed additional feedback loops in the glucose control circuitry may be general enough to contribute to the explanation of other observations that involve rapid onset or remission of diabetes-like phenomena.
source: Finally, the simplicity of such models makes it plausible that the proposed additional feedback loops in the glucose control circuitry may be general enough to contribute to the explanation of other observations that involve rapid onset or remission of diabetes-like phenomena, as discussed above.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader applicability of the model.
